Saving State

Everything you have built so far is &ostateless&r: a variable is always recomputed from the current values of its inputs, so a network has no memory of what happened before. Sometimes you need exactly that memory, for example a lamp that stays on after a button was pressed. In this tutorial, we will use the &lDelayer&r to save state.

A &lDelayer&r remembers the previous values of the &lVariable Card&r in its top slot, and exposes them as a &7List&0. Start by crafting one, attach it to a network with a &lRedstone Reader&r that is targeting a &lButton&r, and insert the reader's &9Boolean&0 card of the aspect that is simply called &lRedstone&r, which is &9True&0 while there is a signal. Next, set the &lCapacity&r to &61&0 in its gui, and leave &lTicks/Operation&r at &61&0.

The &onewest&r value is always the &olast&r element of the &7List&0, so a &lCapacity&r of &61&0 makes the history hold exactly one element: the value of the previous tick. With a larger &lCapacity&r, the first element would be an older value instead. Now write a new &lVariable Card&r using the bottom slots. This card refers to the &lDelayer&r's history.

The trick for saving state is a &ofeedback loop&r: put a &lVariable Card&r in the &lDelayer&r whose value depends on the &lDelayer&r's own history. Each tick, the &lDelayer&r evaluates that card and stores the result, which becomes the previous value on the next tick. This dependency must be &oindirect&r: putting the history card itself in the top slot only gives an error that the variable is referring to itself. Let's use this to build a &olatch&r: a lamp that is switched on by one &lButton&r, and switched off by another.

Every operator you apply in the &lLogic Programmer&r results in its &oown&r &lVariable Card&r, so we will build the latch from several small cards. You can find each operator by typing its name in the search field. Start by reading the two &lButtons&r with &lRedstone Readers&r as &9Boolean&0 &lRedstone&r cards named &oOn&r and &oOff&r. As the &lGet Or Default&r operator takes all of its inputs as cards, also create an &6Integer&0 card with value &60&0 and a &9Boolean&0 card with value &9False&0. Now define &oPrevious&r as &lGet Or Default&r of the history card, that &6Integer&0 and that &9Boolean&0, so that it also works while the history is still empty.

Next, define &oNotOff&r as &lNot&r &oOff&r, then &oKeep&r as &oPrevious&r &lAnd&r &oNotOff&r, and finally &oState&r as &oOn&r &lOr&r &oKeep&r. Take the reader card out of the &lDelayer&r's top slot, and place &oState&r there instead. All other cards, including the intermediate ones, must be placed in a &lVariable Store&r, as the network can otherwise not find them. Finally, create a second &lVariable Card&r named &oState&r by building that same &lOr&r expression once more, as the first one has to stay in the &lDelayer&r, and insert it into the &lRedstone&r aspect of a &lRedstone Writer&r that is targeting a &lRedstone Lamp&r. The lamp will now stay on after pressing &oOn&r, until you press &oOff&r.

For the final part, we will make a &otoggle&r that flips on every press of a &osingle&r &lButton&r: the &oOn&r one. If we would simply invert &oPrevious&r while the &lButton&r is pressed, the state would flip on every tick of the press. We therefore need to detect the exact tick in which the &lButton&r &obecomes&r pressed. Place a second &lDelayer&r with &lCapacity&r &62&0, so that its history holds the two most recent values. Write a new &lRedstone&r card of that &lButton&r into its top slot, as the earlier &oOn&r card has to stay in the &lVariable Store&r, and write its history card. This history is exactly &7[False, True]&0 in the tick after the &lButton&r was pressed.

Create a static &7List&0 of the &9Booleans&0 &9False&0 and &9True&0, in that order, and define &oEdge&r as the second &lDelayer&r's history card &lEquals&r that &7List&0. Next, define &oNotPrevious&r as &lNot&r &oPrevious&r, and &oState&r as &lChoice&r of &oEdge&r, &oNotPrevious&r and &oPrevious&r. Place it in the top slot of the first &lDelayer&r, which must still have &lCapacity&r &61&0, insert a second copy into the &lRedstone Writer&r, and put the new cards in the &lVariable Store&r. Every press of the &lButton&r now toggles the lamp. Feedback loops like these can save any kind of value, not just &9Booleans&0, so you can now build counters, timers and much more.

Shift-clicking on an input slot inside the &lLogic Programmer&r allows you to configure detailed properties of this input slot. For example, it allows you to indicate if NBT should be considered or not, if this item can be reused across multiple recipes (e.g. if it will not be fully consumed after the crafting job), and if tag-based alternatives should be considered for this item.
Expressions can be combined using ”&&” (and), ”||” (or), and ”!” (not).
For example, applying the expression &4”$.a[?(@ == 3 || (@ == 5))]”&0 on the &3NBT&0 tag &3{ a: [0,1,2,3,4,5] }&0 will output &3[3,5]&0.
Settings
Most parts have a &lSettings&r screen using which basic part settings can be modified.
The Target Side is the side that this part will interact with. It defaults to the opposite of the side of the cable this part was placed upon.
The Ticks/Operation allows you to configure the ticking frequency of this part. The higher, the slower it operates.
The Priority determines the order in which this part is executed within a single network tick.
The Energy Channel indicates the channel from which energy should be consumed when this part ticks. This is only applicable if energy consumption for networks is enabled.

The configuration of a part can be copied to other parts using a &lWrench&r. Shift+right-clicking a part copies it into the Wrench, and right-clicking another part pastes it. The Wrench mode picks what is copied: &lCopy All&r takes everything and only pastes onto a part of the same type, &lCopy Settings&r takes the update interval, priority, channel, side and offsets, and &lCopy Aspect&r takes the active aspect with its variable card and all aspect settings. The last two can be pasted onto any part. Only settings that you changed yourself are copied, so pasting never resets anything you left alone. Each pasted variable card consumes one blank &lVariable Card&r from your inventory, and raising the maximum offset of a part consumes &lOffset Enhancements&r.

Right-clicking with a &lWrench&r that holds a configuration, while not pointing at a part, opens a screen that lists everything it is going to paste: the part settings, the aspect that the copied part was writing with its variable card, and every aspect setting that was changed. Anything in that list can be switched off, so that pasting leaves that part of the target alone, and the button next to the screen switches everything on or off at once. A variable card that the target part already holds is left as it is, so it costs you no blank card.
Offsets
By default, parts will target the direct neighboring position. However, when &lPart Enhancements&r are applied, the target position can be changed through the part's &lOffset&r screen.
Offsets are always relative to the part's target position, and are limited by the number of Part Enhancements that have been applied.

Offsets can either be set manually, or they can be set visually using the &lWrench&r. When setting the &lWrench&r to offset-mode, a position can be stored by shift + right-clicking. This position can be saved into parts by right-clicking them with that &lWrench&r.
Offsets can not only be statically defined, buy they can also be &odynamic&r using &lVariable Cards&r.

The two encode buttons next to the &lMaterializer&r place its materialized value on your clipboard as an encoded string, so that you can share it with other players, or use it in another world. The first button gives a readable encoding, the second a shorter one that is easier to send around.

The &lDecode Value&r element turns a value that was encoded in a &lMaterializer&r into a Variable Card, when it is pasted into its text field. This way, values can be shared between players and worlds. Inside a network, the &lEncode&r, &lEncode Compressed&r and &lDecode&r operators do the same with strings.
Players with operator status have access to the &lNetwork Diagnostics&r tool, which allows the tick time across all networks on the server to be inspected.
To enable this tool, the command &o\integrateddynamics networkdiagnostics&r can be executed, which will start a temporary local web server.

When clicking on the link shown after executing the command, your Web browser will open, and will show a table containing all networks and their elements. You can click on any row to highlight them in the world, or click on the &lTeleport&r button to teleport your player to them.
